    Recommender Systems · Chapter 5

    Collaborative filtering: memory-based, item-based CF

    This interactive course follows the slides of Chapter 5. In Chapter 4 we compared users (rows of the rating matrix). Here we compare items (columns), with the same tools and the same example, so you can compare the two methods side by side.

    Problem

    Same question, another point of view

    We keep the same table and the same question as in Chapter 4. Instead of asking "who rates like Alice?", we ask "which movies are rated like Inception?". If Alice rated those movies highly, she will probably rate Inception highly too, and the other way round.

    Which question does item-based CF ask to predict Alice's rating for Inception?

    The questions this chapter answers

    Five questions, one per part. Q1 is the idea, Q2 the formulas, Q3 the worked example, Q4 the practical choice a real platform has to make, and Q5 the limits that lead to the next chapter on model-based methods.

    Common thread · 1/4

    From rows to columns

    On the left, user-based CF compares two rows: Alice and Bob. On the right, item-based CF compares two columns: Matrix and Inception. The table is the same; only the direction of reading changes. Two movies are similar if the same users gave them similar ratings.
    Common thread · 2/4

    Mirror concepts: one table, two readings

    Every notion of Chapter 4 has a mirror. The user's mean becomes the item's mean. The weight between two users becomes the weight between two items. The neighbours are no longer the users who rated the item, but the items the user rated.
    User-based (Ch. 4)Item-based (Ch. 5)
    We compare…rows (users)columns (items)
    Mean usedr̄i = the USER's meanr̄j = the ITEM's mean
    Weightw(i, i') between two usersw(j, j') between two items
    Neighboursusers who rated item jitems rated by user i
    Sentence“Users similar to you also liked…”“Because you rated Matrix highly…”
    Common thread · 3/4

    Four steps, always the same

    The four steps are those of Chapter 4, applied to columns. Compute the mean of each movie, subtract it from its ratings, measure how similar two movies are with Pearson, then predict from the movies the user already rated.
    Common thread · 4/4

    3 questions to ask on every section

    DATA: still only the rating matrix, read by columns. SCORE: the item's mean plus what this user thinks of similar items. LIMIT: new users and new items have no rating, and the recommendations can become too obvious.

    1 · DATA

    the rating matrix, read by columns

    2 · SCORE

    item mean + weighted deviations

    3 · LIMIT

    cold start, obvious recommendations
    01

    Item-based CF: the idea

    “Users who rated this item highly also rated…”: compare columns instead of rows.

    Explanation

    Item-item CF: users who rated this item highly also rated…

    Start from an item, look at who rated it highly, and see what else those users rated highly. Fahrenheit 451 and The Time Machine received 5 stars from the same readers, so they are "similar". Nothing in the content of the books is used, only the ratings.

    Example

    John, Robert and Jenny gave 5★ to Fahrenheit 451 AND to The Time Machine. Tom buys Fahrenheit 451 → recommend The Time Machine.The books are similar because of the ratings, not their content.
    Explanation

    Two ways of looking at the problem

    You can understand item-based CF from scratch (compare movies by their ratings) or as a copy of user-based CF on the columns. Both views lead to the same formulas. Keep the second view in mind: it makes the whole chapter easy.

    1 · Intuitive

    Start from scratch: compare items by how users rated them.

    2 · Conceptual

    Same principle as user-based CF, but applied to COLUMNS instead of rows.
    Recap

    Recap: user-user CF looks at rows

    In Chapter 4 each user was a row vector. Two users were similar when their rows were close, and the prediction started from the user's own mean. This slide recalls the formula so that you can compare it with the item version on the next slides.
    Explanation

    Item-item CF looks at columns

    Now each item is a column vector, with one rating per user. Two items are similar when their columns are close, i.e. when the same users rated them in the same way. In the picture, the two highlighted columns are compared on the users who rated both.
    • What if we look column-wise instead?
    • Find 2 items that are similar.
    • They are similar if their column vectors are close: users gave them similar ratings.
    Example

    Power Rangers and Transformers

    Look at the two first columns: users 1 and 2 rate both movies high, users 3 and 4 rate both low. Their Pearson correlation is about 0.97. So a user who rates Power Rangers highly will probably rate Transformers highly too. We never looked at what the movies are about.
    Power RangersTransformersNinja Turtles
    User 14.554

    User 3120.5
    User 4220.5

    A user gives 5★ to Power Rangers. What will he probably give to Transformers?

    02

    Item formulas

    Item mean, item-item Pearson weight, and the item score.

    Formula

    Item correlation: the weight between two items

    Same Pearson formula as before, but on columns. The sum runs over the users who rated both items. The big trap: r̄j is the mean of the ITEM, not of the user. In user-based CF we subtract the user's mean; in item-based CF we subtract the item's mean.

    What changes vs Chapter 4

    Ωjj' = users who rated BOTH itemsr̄j = the ITEM's mean (not the user's!)
    Formula

    Item score: the prediction formula

    The prediction starts from the mean of the item we predict. Then we look at the items the user has rated: if he rated them above the crowd and they are similar to our item, the prediction goes up. If they are opposite to our item, it goes down.

    Read it

    r̄j = mean of the item we predict · rij' − r̄j' = how user i rated j' compared to everyone · wjj' = how similar j is to j' · Ψi = items user i rated
    Comparison

    User-user or item-item: why is this item chosen?

    User-based says: people like you rated this highly. Item-based says: you rated similar items highly. The second explanation refers to movies the user already knows, which is why many platforms show "Because you watched…".

    User-user CF

    items rated highly by SIMILAR USERS · “Users like you also liked…”

    Item-item CF

    the user rated SIMILAR ITEMS highly · “Because you rated Matrix highly…”
    Another perspective

    Flip the matrix: items have tastes too

    Turn the table by 90 degrees: items become rows and users become columns. Now the user-based algorithm finds "items that like the same users": that is item-based CF. In code, item-based CF is user-based CF applied to the transposed matrix.
    Try it · flip the rating matrix
    Exercise 2

    Item means and item deviations

    Compute each column mean using only the users who rated the movie. Then subtract the column mean from each rating of that column. These numbers say how a user rated the movie compared to the crowd.

    Matrix (5+4+1+2)/4 = 3.0 · Avatar (3+2+1)/3 = 2.0 · Titanic (4+4+2)/3 ≈ 3.33 · Inception (3+4+5)/3 = 4.0 · Toy Story (2+1+5+4)/4 = 3.0. Bob on Toy Story: 1 − 3.0 = −2.0.

    Alice and Inception again, but item-based.

    Example · data

    Step 2: item-centered deviations

    Each rating minus the mean of its movie. Alice rated Matrix 2 points above the crowd, Avatar 1 point above, Titanic 0.67 above, and Toy Story 1 point below. These four numbers are her opinion compared to everybody else.

    Example · weights

    Step 3: similarity of Inception with Matrix and Avatar

    Compare the Inception column with the Matrix column on the users who rated both: Bob, Carol, Dave. Most products are negative, so the similarity is negative (−0.58). Inception and Avatar share only Carol and Dave: with 2 users Pearson is always ±1, here −1.0.
    Try it · the similarity between any two movies
    Try this: Inception–Matrix (−0.58), Inception–Avatar (−1.00, only 2 users!), Inception–Titanic (−0.45), Inception–Toy Story (+0.71).
    Example · prediction

    Step 4: predict Alice's rating for Inception

    Multiply each similarity by Alice's deviation on that movie. All four products are negative: she rated highly the movies that are opposite to Inception, and rated low the one that resembles it. The weighted deviation is −1.16, so 4.0 − 1.16 ≈ 2.84.

    r̂ = 4.0 + (−3.16 / 2.73) ≈ 2.84 ★ — all four contributions are negative: not a good recommendation for Alice.
    Simulator

    User-based vs item-based on the same question

    Two different routes on the same table: user-based starts from Alice's mean and her similar users, item-based starts from Inception's mean and Alice's similar movies. The numbers differ (2.68 and 2.84) but the decision is the same: do not recommend Inception.

    Exercise 3

    Similarity between Avatar and Matrix

    List the users who rated both movies, take their item deviations, multiply them pairwise and follow the Pearson recipe. Bob did not rate Avatar, so he is not used. The sign of the result tells you if the two movies are rated alike.

    Common users: Alice, Carol, Dave. Avatar devs (+1, 0, −1), Matrix devs (+2, −2, −1). Products +2, 0, +1 → 3. Denominator √2 × 3 ≈ 4.243. sim ≈ +0.71.

    Exercise 4

    Predict Bob's rating for Avatar, item-based

    Bob rated four movies: those are the neighbour items. Compute his deviation on each one, multiply by its similarity with Avatar, add, and divide by the sum of the absolute similarities. Then add the mean of Avatar.

    Similarities with Avatar: Matrix +0.71 · Titanic +0.45 · Inception −1.00 · Toy Story −0.58. Avatar's mean = 2.0.

    Deviations: Matrix +1.0, Titanic +0.67, Inception −1.0, Toy Story −2.0. Products +0.71 + 0.30 + 1.00 + 1.15 = +3.16; Σ|sim| = 2.73. r̂ = 2.0 + 1.16 ≈ 3.16 (user-based: 3.57).

    04

    User-based vs item-based

    More data, faster, more accurate… but less diverse.

    Practical differences

    More data per weight with items

    On a real platform there are many more users than items. Two users rarely rate the same movies, but two popular movies are rated by thousands of the same users. So item-item weights rest on much more data and are more reliable. Our 4-user toy table is the exception.

    Comparing 2 USERS

    up to ~20K items to look at, but each user rated few of them

    Comparing 2 ITEMS

    up to ~100K users to look at; popular items have thousands of ratings
    Practical differences

    Item-based CF is faster

    User-based needs N² weights, each costing M; item-based needs M² weights, each costing N. With 100,000 users and 20,000 items, N² is 25 times larger than M². Squares grow fast: this is why item-based CF is the usual choice for big catalogues.
    User-basedItem-based
    WeightsN²M²
    Cost of eachO(M)O(N)
    TotalO(N²M)O(M²N)
    Try it · user-user vs item-item cost
    Exercise 5

    How much faster is item-based?

    Count the weights for each method (N² and M²), convert them into gigabytes with 4 bytes per weight, then compare the total costs N²M and M²N. The ratio of the two costs is simply N/M.

    N = 100,000 users · M = 20,000 movies · 4 bytes per weight.

    N² = 10¹⁰ × 4 B = 40 GB; M² = 4 × 10⁸ × 4 B = 1.6 GB (25× less). N²M / M²N = N / M = 5.

    Summary

    Flip the matrix: user-user becomes item-item

    Flipping the table turns one algorithm into the other. Item-based is usually more accurate because each item-item weight uses many users. In the picture, Movies 2 and 3 always receive the same ratings, so Bob's 5 for Movie 2 predicts a 5 for Movie 3.
    • Flip the matrix → user-user code becomes item-item code.
    • Item-based CF is generally more accurate: its weights use many users.
    • Movies 2 and 3 always get the same ratings → Bob's 5 for Movie 2 predicts 5 for Movie 3.
    Summary

    Do we care about accuracy? The diversity problem

    A lower MSE is not the only goal. Item-based CF tends to recommend "more of the same": very safe, very obvious items. User-based CF is less accurate but brings more surprise, because your neighbours have other tastes too. Platforms often mix both.

    Item-based

    lower MSE, but obvious recommendations: “more of the same”

    User-based

    higher MSE, but more surprise: your neighbours have other tastes too

    A platform wants users to DISCOVER new genres. Which method is the better base?

    Summary

    The prediction is a linear regression

    Look at the shape of the formula: a weighted sum of input deviations gives an output deviation. That is a linear regression. Here the weights are computed with Pearson; if we learn them from the data instead, we move to model-based CF, the topic of the next chapter.
    Summary

    Not only movies and ratings

    Ratings are rare: most users never rate. But they view, buy, like and share all the time. The same matrix can hold these implicit signals, and the same CF formulas apply. Adding the context (time, place, device) gives context-aware recommender systems.

    Explicit

    ratings: rare (sparse)

    Implicit

    views, purchases, likes, shares

    Context

    time, place, device → context-aware RS

    Limits

    Limits of memory-based collaborative filtering

    Memory-based methods are simple but heavy: all the weights must be stored and recomputed when the data changes. And they are blind to newcomers: a new user or a new item has no rating, so no neighbour. Model-based CF learns compact representations to go further.

    Memory

    simple algorithm, but all the weights are kept in memory

    Computation

    N² or M² weights to compute and store

    Cold start

    nothing to say about a new user or a new item
    ✓

    Summary & final quiz

    Back to the five questions of the chapter, then ten questions to check yourself.

    Summary

    Back to our questions: what we learned

    Item-based CF is user-based CF on the columns: item means, item-item Pearson weights, and a prediction from the movies the user rated. It is faster and usually more accurate on real data, but less diverse, and like all memory-based methods it fails for newcomers.
